newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Sinn Fein blames Major for latest IRA killing.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein blames Major for latest IRA killing.

text.p: Sinn Fein, the political wing of IRA guerrillas accused of slaying a British soldier, on Thursday blamed British Prime Minister John Major for his death.
Spokesmen for the party said Major was personally responsible for the single bullet which ended 23-year-old Stephen Restorick's life.

"John Major has responsibility for collapse of the peace process," Sinn Fein chairman Mitchell McLaughlin told lunchtime news in the Irish republic, with which the IRA seeks to merge Northern Ireland through its 28-year war against British rule.
He used the same analysis in a radio interview in Northern Ireland, where Restorick was killed while serving with Britain's 18,000 troops in the province.

Sinn Fein says it is a separate organisation from the underground IRA. The party does not condone violence but its leaders say they "understand" those who resort to force to end British rule of the province.

The also refuse to condemn IRA attacks -- spokesmen always say they will not "engage in the politics of condemnation" but express regret about hurt caused in what they see as a liberation struggle against a colonial power.

"I think if it (the killing) focuses people's attention on the tragic consequences of political failure then that soldier's young life will not have been in vain," party chairman McLaughlin told BBC radio Ulster.

He took the same line on Ireland's RTE network, which banned Sinn Fein from the airwaves for 25 years for links with the IRA but then allowed its spokesmen airtime when the IRA called a ceasefire in September 1994.

Would the soldier's death advance the cause of Irish republicans? his Dublin interlocutor asked. "Well, with respect, I think the question we have to ask is 'could it have been avoided?'" countered McLaughlin.
By his analysis, and that of Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams, Major's refusal to invite Sinn Fein to Belfast peace talks until the IRA ends its war is the reason the war goes on.
They say Major "squandered" an opportunity for peace by insisting throughout the ceasefire that the IRA show willing to disarm to earn Sinn Fein a seat at peace talks.

The "cessation" ended a year ago when the IRA bombed London's Canary Wharf to protest against Sinn Fein's exclusion from the negotiating process, which is dominated by Sinn Fein's Unionist foes, who want Northern Ireland to stay British.

Sinn Fein in October presented the British government through mediator John Hume with "fresh proposals" for a second ceasefire that said talks without preconditions and a time frame for the negotiations would silence IRA guns.
Major dismissed them and toughened his stand, saying that only a permanent end to the war and proof of the IRA's commitment to democratic means would be enough.

"What I am saying is that John Major is responsible for the fact that the conflict continued and that cessations which we had engineered, which we had developed arguments to sustain, was rejected by John Major," said McLaughlin.
Had that happend, reasoned the Sinn Fein chairman, then neither Restorick, nor the soldier killed in an IRA bomb at Britain's Northern Irleand army HQ last October would have died.
"We could have been into the fourth month of a resumed IRA cessation and that young soldier, and the other soldier, would not have been killed had John Major responded," he said.

Rounding on Major, who faces defeat in elections due by May, McLaughlin -- like Adams -- accused Britain of bowing to demands of Unionists on IRA disarmament to save his political skin in parliament, where he does not have a majority.

So where was the flaw in Sinn Fein's peace process? "Where was the flaw, where was the difficulty? -- it was at Westminister and in John Major's obsession with staying in power and reliance on the Unionists," McLaughlin said.
